classification.difficultyReason: Connect the areas of squares and the missing rectangular area to the middle term in a perfect-square expansion.

content.prompt: Maria has two pieces of paper. One is $10\text{ cm}\times10\text{ cm}$ and the other is $6\text{ cm}\times6\text{ cm}$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Is it possible for these two square pieces of paper to cover a square of size $16\text{ cm}\times16\text{ cm}$ completely?

answer.short: No. The pieces have a total area of $136\text{ cm}^2$, less than the required $256\text{ cm}^2$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}10^2+6^2&=100+36\\10^2+6^2&=136\\16^2&=256\end{align*}$$
The two pieces provide $136\text{ cm}^2$ of paper. Since $136<256$, they cannot cover the larger square completely.

children.label: b
children.prompt: How does the answer to part a show that $(10+6)^2\ne10^2+6^2$?

answer.short: The larger square has area $(10+6)^2=256\text{ cm}^2$, while the two pieces have total area $10^2+6^2=136\text{ cm}^2$. These areas are unequal.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}(10+6)^2&=16^2\\(10+6)^2&=256\\10^2+6^2&=136\end{align*}$$
The pieces do not cover the larger square because their total area is smaller. Thus $(10+6)^2\ne10^2+6^2$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: How much more paper is needed to cover the $16\text{ cm}\times16\text{ cm}$ square?

answer.short: $120\text{ cm}^2$: two $6\text{ cm}\times10\text{ cm}$ rectangles of paper.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}16^2-(10^2+6^2)&=256-136\\16^2-(10^2+6^2)&=120\end{align*}$$
An additional $120\text{ cm}^2$ is needed. Two $6\text{ cm}\times10\text{ cm}$ rectangles provide this area.

children.label: d
children.prompt:
How does your answer to part c reinforce the result that
$$(10+6)^2=10^2+2\times10\times6+6^2?$$

answer.short: The extra $120\text{ cm}^2$ equals $2\times10\times6$, the area of the two missing rectangles. Adding it to the two square areas gives the whole square.
answer.worked:
The two missing rectangles each have area $10\times6=60\text{ cm}^2$, so together they contribute the middle term $2\times10\times6=120\text{ cm}^2$.
$$\begin{align*}(10+6)^2&=10^2+2\times10\times6+6^2\\(10+6)^2&=100+120+36\\(10+6)^2&=256\end{align*}$$
